title: Integration Testing
description: Learn to write integration tests for ASP.NET Core APIs using WebApplicationFactory and TestServer. Understand how to test the full HTTP pipeline, use a real or in-memory database, and verify end-to-end request behavior.

blocks.text: Integration testing sits between unit testing and end-to-end testing. While unit tests mock everything, integration tests let real components interact — the full HTTP pipeline runs, routing resolves, controllers execute, and (optionally) a real database is used. This catches bugs that mocks would never reveal, such as serialization issues, routing typos, and configuration mistakes.

ASP.NET Core provides WebApplicationFactory, a helper class from the Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing package that starts your application in-memory for testing. It creates a TestServer — a lightweight, in-process web server — and gives you an HttpClient that sends real HTTP requests to it. The entire pipeline, from routing to response serialization, runs exactly as it would in production.

WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> bootstraps your application using the Program.cs or Startup.cs from your main project. It creates a new host, wires up middleware, and exposes a CreateClient() method that returns an HttpClient pointing at the in-memory server. Because it uses your real Program.cs, any configuration, services, or middleware you have registered are all active during the test.

blocks.title: WebApplicationFactory Creates a Real Host
blocks.text: WebApplicationFactory does not mock Program.cs. It runs your actual startup logic, so if your DI registrations, middleware order, or route configuration have bugs, integration tests will catch them. This is exactly what makes integration testing so valuable.

Create a separate test project in your solution. Install three NuGet packages: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing for WebApplicationFactory, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory for an in-memory database, and xunit with the Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk runner. Your test project should reference your main API project.

blocks.title: Test Project csproj Configuration
blocks.content: The minimum .csproj configuration for an ASP.NET Core integration test project.
blocks.code:
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.NET.Sdk">

  <PropertyGroup>
    <TargetFramework>net8.0</TargetFramework>
    <ImplicitUsings>enable</ImplicitUsings>
    <Nullable>enable</Nullable>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing" Version="8.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory" Version="8.0.0" />
    <PackageReference Include="xunit" Version="2.6.2" />
    <PackageReference Include="xunit.runner.visualstudio" Version="2.5.4" />
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk" Version="17.8.0" />
  </ItemGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <ProjectReference Include="..\MyApi\MyApi.csproj" />
  </ItemGroup>

</Project>

blocks.text: Integration tests implement IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>. The fixture creates one shared instance of the factory for the entire test class, meaning the application starts once and all tests reuse it. The factory's CreateClient() gives you an HttpClient that sends real HTTP requests to the in-memory server.

blocks.text: Using a Real Database for Integration Tests

For more realistic integration tests, you can use a real database instead of mocks. The in-memory provider (Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory) is convenient but does not enforce relational constraints or use real SQL. For SQL Server or SQLite, use a test-specific connection string that points to a database created and destroyed for each test run.

A common pattern is to use SQLite in-memory mode for integration tests. It supports real SQL and relational constraints while remaining fast and isolated. You configure your DbContext to use SQLite during tests and seed known data before each test.

blocks.text: Integration tests validate the boundaries between components. They confirm that routing correctly maps URLs to controller actions, that model binding populates action parameters, that the controller calls the service layer, and that the response is serialized correctly. They do not test individual method logic — that is the job of unit tests.

blocks.title: What Integration Tests Verify
items: Route templates correctly match incoming request URLs to controller actions
Middleware (authentication, authorization, CORS) runs and behaves as expected
Model binding converts request data into the correct action parameters
Controllers return the correct status codes and response shapes
Response serialization (JSON) matches the expected schema
Database operations (with a real DB) correctly persist and retrieve data

terms.definition: An ASP.NET Core helper that starts your application in-memory for testing and provides a test HttpClient.
The in-process web server created by WebApplicationFactory that handles HTTP requests without network overhead.
An xUnit interface that shares a single fixture instance across all test methods in a class.
A database (SQLite or EF InMemory) that runs in-process during tests, providing realistic data behavior without external infrastructure.
The .NET HTTP client used in integration tests to send real requests to the in-memory TestServer.

blocks.title: Keep Integration Tests Focused
blocks.text: Each integration test should verify one user-facing behavior: 'GET /api/products returns 200 with a list.' If a test fails, the name should make it obvious what broke. Avoid testing multiple endpoints or scenarios in a single test method.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: Integration Testing
points: Integration tests verify how multiple components work together through the real HTTP pipeline
WebApplicationFactory starts your app in-memory, giving you a TestServer and HttpClient
IClassFixture<T> shares one factory instance across all tests in a class for efficiency
Use SQLite in-memory mode for realistic database behavior without external infrastructure
Integration tests catch routing, serialization, and middleware bugs that unit tests miss
Run integration tests in CI/CD alongside unit tests to catch pipeline-level regressions
blocks.takeaway: Integration tests fill the gap between fast unit tests and slow end-to-end tests. With WebApplicationFactory, you get a production-like environment at the cost of seconds per test suite run — an excellent trade-off for catching real-world bugs.

blocks.title: Exercise: Write Integration Tests for the Products API
blocks.description: Create a complete integration test class for the Products API using WebApplicationFactory.
steps: Create a test project with Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Testing and Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.InMemory
Create a CustomWebApplicationFactory that swaps the database for SQLite in-memory mode
Write a test that GETs /api/products and asserts 200 OK with a non-empty list
Write a test that GETs /api/products/1 and asserts 200 OK with the correct product name
Write a test that GETs /api/products/9999 and asserts 404 Not Found
Write a test that POSTs a new product and asserts 201 Created with the correct Location header
Seed the in-memory database with test data before running the tests
blocks.expectedOutcome: A complete integration test class with six test methods covering the full HTTP lifecycle. Tests run against the real pipeline, validate real HTTP status codes, and use a real database for data operations.

items.text: I understand the difference between unit tests and integration tests
items.hint: Unit tests mock dependencies. Integration tests let real components interact.

items.text: I can explain what WebApplicationFactory does
items.hint: It starts your ASP.NET Core app in-memory and gives you an HttpClient to send real requests.

items.text: I know what IClassFixture<T> is for
items.hint: It shares a single factory instance across all tests in a class so the app starts once.

items.text: I can set up a SQLite in-memory database for integration tests

items.text: I know what kinds of bugs integration tests catch that unit tests miss
